title: The fire
hook: Sita walks into the flame and out
carry: the tradition argues about this too

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari's lament, Ravana's queen grieving the man she warned and still loved.

This is the scene people stop at. The war is won. Sita is brought out of Lanka, after all those months in the garden refusing Ravana every day. The whole army crowds around to see her. She comes to Rama. This is the reunion the entire story has been running toward. And it goes wrong. This one doesn't get tidied up. Here it is straight, then what people in the tradition have said about it, because they've been arguing about this scene for a very long time.
screen: `THE REUNION THE STORY RAN TOWARD.` → `AND IT GOES WRONG.` → `NO TIDYING THIS ONE UP.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, Rama speaks coldly, in front of everyone. He says he fought to wipe out the insult to his name, and that since she lived in another man's house, he can't simply take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes. Sita is stunned. Then she answers him, and her answer is magnificent: her heart was always his; what Ravana did to her body was done by force; how could he speak to her like a common man? She turns to Lakshmana and tells him to build a fire, and she walks into the flames. The fire god, Agni, rises out of them carrying her unharmed, and declares her pure. Rama says he never doubted her; he did it, he says, so the world would have no doubt. That's the text: agni pariksha, the trial by fire. Now, how the tradition reads it. Tulsidas, in the Ramcharitmanas, tells it differently: before the abduction, the real Sita was placed in the fire's keeping, and a shadow Sita was the one taken; the fire only gives the real one back. Some devotees take comfort in that. Others read Valmiki's scene as a king bowing to public opinion, and hold that as a flaw, or a tragedy, or a test of dharma under pressure. Women have long sung and retold this story from Sita's side, questioning Rama, like the Bengali poet Chandrabati. Some scholars also point out that a still harder chapter, Sita's later banishment, comes in a book they consider a later addition. None of these voices is outside Hinduism. They're all inside it. This tradition doesn't ask you to stop asking.
screen: `RAMA SPEAKS COLDLY, IN PUBLIC.` · `SITA ANSWERS, AND WALKS INTO THE FIRE.` · `AGNI CARRIES HER OUT.` · `SHADOW SITA, FLAW, OR TEST? ALL INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Don't decide what the scene means; picture Sita walking toward the fire with her back straight, and Rama watching, and let yourself feel whatever comes: anger, confusion, awe, sadness, all felt by people who love this story. Hold the question gently, like something you'll carry, not solve. If someone who grew up with the Ramayana comes to mind, a parent, a friend, let their face stay a moment.
Agni pariksha. The trial by fire. Sita walks into the flame and out, and the argument about it has never stopped.
Your line: the tradition argues about this too. The question is allowed to stay open. Sixty-eight, and counting.

howItsDone: Sita's trial by fire is told and debated openly in Hindu homes, temples and scholarship; devotional tellings such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas present a shadow Sita, while some readers, poets and women's song traditions have questioned the scene from Sita's side.

fork.setup: you're Sita. after months of refusing Ravana, the man you waited for speaks to you coldly in front of an army. what do you do?
options: walk away from Rama, as he offers.
answer him, then ask for a fire to be built.
stay silent and wait for him to change his mind.
fork.reveal: she answers him with dignity, then asks Lakshmana to build a fire, and walks in. Agni brings her out unharmed. what it means is still argued.

original.note: Sanskrit: agni (fire) + pariksha (test). In Hindi today, pariksha also means a school exam.

what a scholar hears: Valmiki's Yuddha Kanda has the trial; Tulsidas has a shadow Sita; some scholars think Sita's later banishment belongs to a later-added book.
